appiah: Kwame Anthony Appiah (born 1954) is a Ghanaian-British-American philosopher who works on ethics, identity, race, and culture. His book Cosmopolitanism argues that we have obligations to strangers far beyond our own communities, and that conversation across difference matters more than eventual agreement. He has also written influentially on honor, lying, and the meanings of race and religion.
ayn-rand: Ayn Rand (1905-1982) was a Russian-American novelist and self-taught philosopher whose 'Objectivism' defends rational self-interest, ethical egoism, and laissez-faire capitalism. Through novels like The Fountainhead and Atlas Shrugged she argued that selfishness, rightly understood, is a virtue; academic philosophers have largely kept her at arm's length, but her cultural influence remains enormous.
bernard-suits: Bernard Suits (1929-2007) was a Canadian philosopher of sport and games whose playful classic The Grasshopper defines game-playing as the voluntary attempt to overcome unnecessary obstacles. He speculated that in a utopia freed from necessity, playing games might be the only thing left worth doing.
bostrom: Nick Bostrom (born 1973) is a Swedish-born philosopher at Oxford who works on existential risk and the future of humanity. He is best known for the simulation argument, which holds that we may well be living in a computer simulation, and for warning that misaligned advanced artificial intelligence could be catastrophic.
clausewitz: Carl von Clausewitz (1780-1831) was a Prussian general and military theorist whose unfinished masterpiece On War made him the West's most quoted strategist. He argued that war is 'the continuation of politics by other means,' and that real war is inherently chaotic, shaped by chance, friction, and the passions of nations.
crenshaw: Kimberle Crenshaw (born 1959) is an American legal scholar and critical race theorist who coined the term 'intersectionality' in 1989 to describe how racism and sexism overlap, leaving Black women, for example, facing harms that neither category alone can capture. The idea has since reshaped law, feminism, and political thought.
edmund-burke: Edmund Burke (1729-1797) was an Irish-born British statesman and philosopher, often called the father of modern conservatism for his scathing defense of tradition and gradual reform against the French Revolution. His early Philosophical Enquiry also popularized the aesthetics of the sublime: terrifying vastness that awes rather than pleases.
empedocles: Empedocles (c. 494-434 BC) was a pre-Socratic Greek philosopher, poet, and physician from Sicily who taught that everything is composed of four eternal 'roots' - earth, water, air, and fire - mixed and separated by two cosmic forces, Love and Strife. He is also credited with an early theory of evolution by survival of the fittest.
gaston-bachelard: Gaston Bachelard (1884-1962) was a French philosopher who wrote on both science and poetry. In philosophy of science he showed how progress demands an 'epistemological break' with past errors, while in The Poetics of Space he explored how attics, cellars, and nests carry our imagination and daydreams.
georges-bataille: Georges Bataille (1897-1962) was a French novelist and philosopher who wrote from the edges - eroticism, sacrifice, the sacred - at once a profound influence on postwar French thought and a scandal to it. His economics of excess held that societies must waste surplus in festival and destruction, defying the sober logic of utility.
goffman: Erving Goffman (1922-1982) was a Canadian-American sociologist who studied face-to-face life as theater. In The Presentation of Self in Everyday Life he showed how we perform roles, manage impressions, and follow subtle stage directions in every interaction - work later drawn on by gender theorists such as Judith Butler.
graham-priest: Graham Priest (born 1948) is a British-born logician and philosopher, now at the City University of New York, famous for defending dialetheism: the view that some contradictions are actually true. Using 'paraconsistent' logics that keep such truths from exploding into chaos, he has reopened questions most logicians considered settled since Aristotle.
huizinga: Johan Huizinga (1872-1945) was a Dutch historian whose 1938 classic Homo Ludens argued that play is older than culture and creates it: law, war, poetry, and philosophy all begin in play. His idea of the 'magic circle' - games as temporary worlds with their own rules - is now central to game studies.
iris-murdoch: Iris Murdoch (1919-1999) was a British novelist and philosopher who made the moral life a matter of attention: the difficult, loving effort to see other people as they really are rather than through the fog of our own ego. Drawing on Plato and Simone Weil, she saw this 'unselfing,' not rules or choices, as the heart of goodness.
josiah-royce: Josiah Royce (1855-1916) was an American absolute idealist at Harvard, a colleague of William James, who argued that individuals become fully themselves only through loyalty to genuine communities. His philosophy of loyalty anticipated later communitarianism, and he made lasting contributions to the problem of error and the nature of community.
mcluhan: Marshall McLuhan (1911-1980) was a Canadian media theorist and literary critic whose aphorism 'the medium is the message' argued that communication technologies reshape human life more than their content does. He foresaw the 'global village' created by electronic media and became a posthumous guru of the internet age.
montaigne: Michel de Montaigne (1533-1592) was a French Renaissance nobleman who invented the personal essay, using it to ask 'What do I know?' A gentle skeptic in the Pyrrhonian tradition, he examined friendship, death, and his own habits with unmatched candor, making self-inquiry itself a philosophical method.
naess: Arne Naess (1912-2009) was a Norwegian philosopher, Spinoza scholar, and avid mountaineer who founded 'deep ecology' in 1973. He argued that nature has intrinsic value independent of human use, criticizing 'shallow' environmentalism that worries about pollution only insofar as it affects affluent people.
plotinus: Plotinus (c. 204-270 AD) was a Greek-speaking Egyptian philosopher, founder of Neoplatonism, who taught in Rome. His Enneads describe all reality as an emanation from 'the One,' a transcendent source beyond being, with the soul's goal a mystical return to unity. His system deeply shaped Christian, Islamic, and Jewish philosophy.
schelling: F.W.J. Schelling (1775-1854) was a German idealist philosopher who, alongside Fichte and Hegel, transformed post-Kantian thought. He gave nature an active role philosophy had denied it, made art the supreme revelation of the absolute, and posed the problem of evil and human freedom with a darkness that anticipates existentialism.
simone-weil: Simone Weil (1909-1943) was a French philosopher, mystic, and political activist who died at thirty-four, weakened by self-imposed austerity in solidarity with occupied France. Her scattered writings on attention, affliction, and the 'gravity' of the world - later collected as Gravity and Grace - influence theology, ethics, and political thought alike.
voltaire: Voltaire (1694-1778), pen name of Francois-Marie Arouet, was the sharpest wit of the French Enlightenment - a playwright, historian, and crusader for toleration against tyranny and superstition. His satire Candide mercilessly mocked Leibniz's claim that ours is 'the best of all possible worlds' in the face of human suffering.
walzer: Michael Walzer (born 1935) is an American political theorist, longtime coeditor of Dissent, best known for Just and Unjust Wars, which reconstructed the moral rules governing when states may fight and how. His 'dirty hands' thesis holds that politicians sometimes must do wrong to do right - and must accept the stain.
zeno-elea: Zeno of Elea (c. 490-430 BC) was a pre-Socratic philosopher and defender of Parmenides, famous for paradoxes - Achilles and the tortoise, the arrow - that seem to prove motion impossible. Aristotle called him the inventor of dialectic, and his puzzles about the infinite still occupy mathematicians and philosophers.
